messages.subject: Double Assignment - IPM Abundance Estimates
parts:
This feels like a really simple question, but looking at IPM code for a day wasn't fruitful. 

In most IPMs, N[t] is assigned from N[t-1] and the relevant demographic rates. But in many abundance estimation models, N is a derived parameter. For example, in the common implementation of SCR, N <- sum(z[1:n]). I'm struggling with how to get around double assignment of variables. The normal approach to integrating count data is passing it as data and modeling it as a result of an observation process where N from the process model is the mean of an observation process. However, if the count or abundance estimate arises as a derived parameter from a component model, I cannot think of a way to tie it back to the process model given that double assignment isn't allowed. Am I missing something obvious?

Cheers,
Kenneth

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: Double Assignment - IPM Abundance Estimates
parts:
Hi Kenneth,
Thanks for the question. I am going to answer it from the perspective of nimble mechanics, not from the perspective of statistical correctness or what you might or should want to do. In many cases where I've seen people's thoughts head towards double declarations (often one deterministic, one stochastic), there is arguably a flaw in the reasoning, but I've also seen some situations where it really can make sense. If you are confident you want to do this, a workaround is to make the stochastic declaration have a dummy data value and the N as a parameter. One would usually do this via a user-defined distribution, but one could also use the Poisson "zeros" trick. It would look like this:

In model code:

dummy ~ dmydist(N, theta) # giving theta as another parameter just make a fuller example

outside the model code:
dmydist <- nimbleFunction(
 run = function(x = double(), N = double(), theta = double(), log = integer(0, default = 0)) {
    # calculate the logProb here, e.g. perhaps from a normal:
    logProb <- dnorm(N, mean = theta, sd = 1, log = TRUE)
    if(log) return(logProb) else return(exp(logProb))
    returnType(double())
})

Notice that "dummy" is never used. It should be provided as data to the model and it will be the "x" input to dmydist, which is never used. It exists to be a node in the model graph (DAG) that depends on N and any other parameters and will contribute a logProb to any model calculations. It will also make N be not strictly a posterior predictive node in the DAG but rather a deterministic parent node to dummy.

I hope that makes sense.
Perry

messages.subject: AW: Double Assignment - IPM Abundance Estimates
parts:
Dear Kenneth,

 

No, you’re not missing anything. Quite on the contrary, as I see it, this is a major challenge for current IPM-ology: that we can’t model (= estimate) N in the same IPM where we specify the demographic model for how N evolves over time as a function of the demographic rates. Somebody should come up with a grand idea and then write a paper about it.

 

Best regards  -- Marc

Hi all,

Thanks for the great question and discussion. It's a somewhat different problem, but it seemed like this approach would also be germane to a type of data imputation issue I'm dealing with and I wanted to make sure I wasn't off-base. 

For example, consider a regression model where y[j]~NB(mean[group[j]], variance[group[j]]) [I recognize this isn't the default nimble parameterization of the NB]. All y[j] are missing for one group. Instead, sampling statistics are reported for that group (y-bar, SE of y-bar) and also predictors, offsets, etc. To try to enforce this from a coding perspective, would it be reasonable to pose that the missing y[j]~NB(mean[group[j]], variance[group[j]]), and, focusing only on the mean for simplicity:

 mean_y_m<-mean(y[missing])
dummy~dcustom(mean_y_m, reported_mean_y_m) 
dcustom<-nimbleFunction{...
...
logProb <- dnorm(mean_y_m, mean = reported_mean_y_m, sd = smallnumber, log = TRUE) ###soft constraint MCMC mean is close to sample mean
...
}

I think there'd be some trade-off between imputation accuracy and statistical efficiency of the MCMC sampling based on whatever the small number argument is above?

Thanks for any insight!

John
